arXiv:2607.27083v1 [cs.LG] 29 Jul 2026

Scores Are Not Decisions: Cost-Aware Stopping for Tool Acquisition in LLM Agents

Yicheng Feng    Yan Zhang    Yan Cheng\corresponding    Wei Qi\corresponding
Abstract

As LLM agents increasingly depend on diverse external services such as search engines, databases, and connectors, agent harnesses face a fundamental tool-selection challenge: acquiring too few tools leaves the task under-informed, while too many adds cost, context load, and privacy exposure. Routers and retrievers can rank candidate tools by relevance, but a ranking alone does not determine how many are worth selecting. Existing approaches leave acquisition under heterogeneous costs unaddressed. We formulate this decision as cost-aware marginal decision-focused stopping (CAM-DF) over ranked tool prefixes, with CAM-DF-lite as a compact interpretable variant. We train directly on the offline gap between stopping now and the best continuation: its sign labels the decision, its magnitude weights each error by the payoff at stake. We prove this objective is Bayes-aligned with the stopping target and that score-only rules are suboptimal under heterogeneous costs. We evaluate on 1,343 tasks across five tool-use domains. On τ\tau-bench Retail, CAM-DF attains the highest payoff among deployable methods, with gains over a predict-then-threshold baseline across all five ranking sources and two cost regimes. Our approach is state-of-the-art under heterogeneous costs and high cost pressure, with larger gains under weaker rankings. In live execution, CAM-DF exposes the agent to 37% fewer tools than full access while maintaining comparable task success. The CAM-DF family is a lightweight pre-execution plugin that turns existing tool rankings into lower-cost acquisition decisions without fine-tuning the underlying LLM.

1 Introduction

As tool ecosystems expand, agent harnesses must decide how much external tool access to provide for each task. Unnecessary tool acquisition can consume context and system resources, add latency and API expense, and increase privacy and error exposure, with these costs accumulating across repeated agent turns. Recent work shows that performance can plateau as tool-call budgets increase (Liu et al. 2025b), while even leading models do not reliably execute cost-optimal tool-use plans as tasks become more complex or tool costs change (Liu et al. 2025a). Agent-evaluation research has accordingly argued that cost should be assessed alongside task performance (Kapoor et al. 2024). This increased focus highlights a central question: when does expanded tool access justify its additional cost?

We examine this question in a general pre-execution setting in which an upstream scoring or routing mechanism supplies a task-specific ranking of candidate tools with heterogeneous costs. Given this ranking, the agent harness must still choose an acquisition depth kk. This depth defines a prefix containing the first kk tools in the ranked list. The ranking establishes the relative priority of candidate tools, but it does not by itself identify whether an individual tool is necessary or whether the selected prefix contains all tools required for the task. Determining where to stop therefore requires comparing the payoff from stopping with the best payoff attainable by continuing. Moreover, when tool costs differ, score-based ranking is provably inconsistent with the optimal acquisition rule (Sec. 4). Prior work instead routes queries among predefined retrieval strategies (Jeong et al. 2024) or learns whether to continue after each round of iterative retrieval (Park et al. 2025). These formulations leave open how to convert a given tool ranking into a cost-aware acquisition depth before execution.

To address this gap, we develop Cost-Aware Marginal Decision-Focused Stopping (CAM-DF), a learned stopping policy over ranked tool prefixes. CAM-DF derives supervision directly from downstream payoff. For task xx and acquired tool set AA, we define U⁡(A,x)=sufficiency⁡(A,x)−λ​∑j∈AcjU(A,x)=\operatorname{sufficiency}(A,x)-\lambda\sum_{j\in A}c_{j}, where sufficiency⁡(A,x)\operatorname{sufficiency}(A,x) indicates whether AA contains the required tools, cjc_{j} denotes tool cost, and λ\lambda controls cost pressure. For each candidate stopping point, we compare the payoff of the current prefix with the highest payoff attainable from any longer prefix. The sign of this payoff gap determines the target decision, while its magnitude weights errors by the payoff at stake. We show that the resulting regret-weighted objective is Bayes-aligned with the offline stopping target. As shown in Figure 1, CAM-DF uses ranking scores, tool costs, and prefix-progress features to select an acquisition depth. The downstream agent then operates with the selected prefix, requiring no modification to the upstream ranking mechanism or the underlying LLM.

We evaluate CAM-DF on 1,343 tasks across five tool-use domains, using τ\tau-bench Retail (Yao et al. 2025) as the primary testbed. CAM-DF achieves the highest mean payoff among deployable methods under both uniform and heterogeneous tool costs. Across five frozen LLM ranking configurations and two cost regimes, it outperforms a feature-matched predict-then-threshold baseline in all ten settings, with 95% paired-bootstrap confidence intervals excluding zero in nine. A tuned score-per-cost threshold remains competitive at λ=0.12\lambda=0.12, but CAM-DF’s advantage becomes clearer at λ=0.20\lambda=0.20; its gains over predict-then-threshold stopping are largest under the weakest ranking configuration. Ablations indicate that marginal-cost features matter most under heterogeneous costs and that learning the payoff gap is more effective than predicting current-prefix sufficiency. Its gains across four additional domains likewise concentrate under heterogeneous costs, although the tuned threshold remains competitive in some regimes. In an end-to-end τ\tau-bench Retail evaluation, CAM-DF reduces pre-execution read-tool exposure from 7 to 4.4 tools (37%) while maintaining comparable observed task success. We further introduce CAM-DF-lite, a lightweight, interpretable variant that retains most of the full policy’s empirical gains.

Our contributions are threefold. First, we formulate tool acquisition as cost-aware stopping over ranked prefixes, enabling acquisition depth to be optimized directly for downstream utility while accounting for task sufficiency and heterogeneous costs. Second, we develop a decision-focused objective with Bayes-alignment guarantees and a marginal value-per-cost analysis that characterizes when score-only acquisition becomes suboptimal. Third, we propose the CAM-DF family of deployable, modular stopping policies, comprising a flexible learned policy and a lightweight, interpretable variant that retains most of the full policy’s empirical gains. Taken together, these contributions position cost-aware stopping as a well-founded and practical control layer for agent harnesses.

2 Related Work

CAM-DF connects research on cost-aware tool use and adaptive ranked-list depth with methodological work on decision-focused learning and costly search.

Tool routing and cost-aware tool use.

Tool-augmented LLM systems support API invocation and candidate retrieval from large catalogs (Schick et al. 2023; Patil et al. 2024; Qin et al. 2024; Du et al. 2024). Work on tool-use control studies tool necessity and selection, on-demand registration, and reductions in unnecessary calls or context exposure (Huang et al. 2024; Ross et al. 2025; Zhang et al. 2024; Qian et al. 2025; Wu et al. 2026; Sun et al. 2026). Cost-aware methods further allocate tools under budgets, generate tool-use plans, or manage exploration costs during sequential execution (Zheng et al. 2024; Wu et al. 2025; Ding et al. 2026; Liu et al. 2026). These studies primarily focus on tool selection, call timing, or budget allocation, without directly modeling acquisition depth after ranking and before execution. CAM-DF adds this control layer to separate tool prioritization from access allocation, enabling task-specific acquisition depth without modifying the upstream ranker or downstream agent.

Adaptive retrieval and ranked-list depth.

Adaptive retrieval regulates evidence gathering using confidence, learned retrieval signals, attention-based information needs, or predicted query complexity (Jiang et al. 2023; Asai et al. 2024; Su et al. 2024; Jeong et al. 2024). Within this literature, two lines are particularly relevant to CAM-DF. The first treats iterative retrieval as a sequential stopping problem and learns whether to continue after each retrieval round (Park et al. 2025). The second learns query-specific cutoffs for retrieval, reranking, and ranked tool descriptions, including joint optimization of order and depth (Bahri et al. 2020; Meng et al. 2024; Sun et al. 2025; Repantis et al. 2026). These lines establish learned stopping and query-specific depth as important control mechanisms, but their objectives do not explicitly balance downstream task sufficiency against heterogeneous acquisition costs. CAM-DF addresses this gap by incorporating both terms into downstream payoff and learning cutoffs from stop-versus-continue regret.

Decision-focused learning.

Decision-focused learning incorporates downstream objectives because statistically similar prediction errors can produce different decision losses (Mandi et al. 2024). Related approaches learn prescriptions directly from contextual data (Ban and Rudin 2019; Bertsimas and Koduri 2022), differentiate through downstream optimization (Donti et al. 2017), develop regret-based surrogate losses (Elmachtoub and Grigas 2022), or adjust fitted estimates for asymmetric payoff effects while preserving modularity (Albert et al. 2025). CAM-DF extends the scope of decision-focused learning to the realm of cost-aware stopping over ranked tool prefixes by deriving a regret target from the payoff difference between the current prefix and its best continuation and establishing its Bayes alignment with the offline stopping target.

Costly search and stopping.

Classical costly-search models compare the expected benefit of an additional observation with its acquisition cost. Weitzman’s Pandora’s-box model uses reservation values to determine a fixed inspection order and an outcome-adaptive stopping rule (Weitzman 1979). Subsequent work considers constrained inspection orders, utilities over multiple discovered values, and contextual learning of search policies (Beyhaghi and Cai 2023; Boodaghians et al. 2023; Olszewski and Weber 2015; Atsidakou et al. 2024). Recent LLM applications use sequential stopping to control repeated generation and API cascades after observing intermediate outputs (Kalayci et al. 2025; Belloni et al. 2026). CAM-DF introduces a pre-execution, set-level formulation of costly stopping for complementary tool access, in which the selected prefix is fixed before any tool output is observed.

3 Problem Formulation

Setting.

We consider a black-box acquisition layer around a tool-using service agent within a single agent turn, using only public signals and requiring no access to the agent’s internals. The layer receives a candidate set 𝒯={1,…,m}\mathcal{T}=\{1,\dots,m\}, an upstream ranking over those candidates, and a cost cj>0c_{j}>0 for calling each tool jj; costs may be homogeneous (cj≡1c_{j}\equiv 1) or heterogeneous. It walks the ranking, chooses a prefix, and hands that prefix to the agent to execute. The prefix is fixed before the first tool runs, so the decision rests only on the ranking, the costs, and the layer’s own acquisition progress. Such a ranking is readily available in modern harnesses and may come from any upstream component that orders tools: a retriever, router, scoring prompt, workflow rule, or offline shadow-labeling pass. Each task xx has a minimal required-tool set Gx⊆𝒯G_{x}\subseteq\mathcal{T}. An acquired set AA is sufficient if and only if Gx⊆AG_{x}\subseteq A. Tools in A∖GxA\setminus G_{x} do not change task sufficiency but incur additional acquisition cost. GxG_{x} is a latent property of the task and is unavailable to the acquisition layer at decision time. For logged tasks, it is available through benchmark annotations and used only offline to construct training labels and evaluation metrics.

In our empirical replay we populate the ranking interface with frozen LLM scoring prompts that see only the task text xx and tool descriptions djd_{j},

sj(x)=h(x,dj)∈[0,1],j=1,…,m.s_{j}(x)=h(x,d_{j})\in[0,1],\qquad j=1,\dots,m. (1)

This scorer plays the role a retrieval or routing stage plays in deployed stacks (Qin et al. 2024; Du et al. 2024). The scores rank tools by estimated necessity but are not calibrated membership probabilities Pr⁡(j∈Gx∣x,dj)\Pr(j\in G_{x}\mid x,d_{j}), and the problem is converting them into an acquisition decision.

Payoff.

For an acquired set A⊆𝒯A\subseteq\mathcal{T} on task xx, the payoff is U⁡(A,x)=v⁡(A,Gx)−λ​∑j∈AcjU(A,x)=v(A,G_{x})-\lambda\sum_{j\in A}c_{j}, where v⁡(A,Gx)∈[0,1]v(A,G_{x})\in[0,1] is the task value assigned to AA, and λ>0\lambda>0 is the cost pressure, measured as the price of one unit of tool cost in units of task value. Under exact sufficiency, v(A,Gx)=𝟏{Gx⊆A}v(A,G_{x})=\mathbf{1}\{G_{x}\subseteq A\}, yielding

Uexact(A,x)=𝟏{Gx⊆A}−λ∑j∈Acj.U_{\mathrm{exact}}(A,x)=\mathbf{1}\{G_{x}\subseteq A\}-\lambda\sum_{j\in A}c_{j}. (2)

The indicator equals one when AA contains all required tools and zero otherwise. Tools acquired beyond GxG_{x} add cost but no task value, whereas omitting any required tool makes AA insufficient. As a robustness specification, we also use partial coverage, v⁡(A,Gx)=|A∩Gx|/|Gx|v(A,G_{x})=|A\cap G_{x}|/|G_{x}|, yielding Upartial​(A,x)=|A∩Gx|/|Gx|−λ​∑j∈AcjU_{\mathrm{partial}}(A,x)=|A\cap G_{x}|/|G_{x}|-\lambda\sum_{j\in A}c_{j}, which assigns partial credit to acquired required tools and represents tasks whose value accumulates across multiple pieces of information (Table A11). Both value functions are nondecreasing in AA; acquisition costs enter separately through the penalty term.

Stopping along the score ranking.

Order the tools by score, s(1)​(x)≥⋯≥s(m)​(x)s_{(1)}(x)\geq\cdots\geq s_{(m)}(x), and let At={(1),…,(t)}A_{t}=\{(1),\dots,(t)\} denote the prefix of the first tt tools. The policy chooses a stopping depth t∈{0,…,m}t\in\{0,\dots,m\}: at each state StS_{t} (the situation after acquiring the first tt tools) it either stops with AtA_{t} or acquires the next-ranked tool. Restricting to score-ordered prefixes keeps the upstream interface unchanged and reduces a 2m2^{m} subset choice to m+1m{+}1 nested decisions.

Observable state and model input.

The policy input XtX_{t} at state StS_{t} contains variables observable at decision time: the scores and costs of selected and remaining tools, score gaps, acquisition progress, and λ\lambda. Because GxG_{x} is latent at decision time, variables derived from GxG_{x} are unavailable as inputs: the required set itself, |Gx||G_{x}|, the rank needed to cover GxG_{x}, or missing-required indicators. We use the annotated GxG_{x} only offline, to construct training labels, regret weights, and evaluation metrics.

Stopping target.

At state StS_{t}, the policy either stops with the current prefix AtA_{t} or continues. Let the stop payoff be Qstop​(St)=U⁡(At,x)Q_{\mathrm{stop}}(S_{t})=U(A_{t},x) and the best-continuation payoff be Qcontinue​(St)=maxk>t⁡U⁡(Ak,x)Q_{\mathrm{continue}}(S_{t})=\max_{k>t}U(A_{k},x), and define the decision gap

Δ⁡(St)=Qstop​(St)−Qcontinue​(St).\Delta(S_{t})=Q_{\mathrm{stop}}(S_{t})-Q_{\mathrm{continue}}(S_{t}). (3)

Stopping is optimal exactly when continuing cannot do better, i.e., when Δ⁡(St)≥0\Delta(S_{t})\geq 0. This defines the target stop/continue label yt∗=𝟏{Δ(St)≥0}y_{t}^{*}=\mathbf{1}\{\Delta(S_{t})\geq 0\}, and |Δ⁡(St)||\Delta(S_{t})| is the payoff lost by choosing the wrong action at StS_{t}. For a fixed task and ranking, yt∗=1y_{t}^{*}=1 exactly when the current prefix is optimal among the current and all later prefixes. The best attainable payoff is maxk⁡U⁡(Ak,x)\max_{k}U(A_{k},x), and Δ⁡(St)\Delta(S_{t}) measures how far the current prefix falls short of the best later one. Both Δ⁡(St)\Delta(S_{t}) and yt∗y_{t}^{*} depend on GxG_{x}, so they are computable on logged tasks but not at the decision time (Lemma 1 in the appendix gives the deterministic characterization of the optimal depth).

4 Theory

One alignment theorem and three structural propositions (proofs in Appendix A) pin down what a learned stopping policy must represent and which features carry the decision.

4.1 From Local Errors to Prefix Regret

For a fixed task and ranking, let Ft=maxk≥t⁡U⁡(Ak,x)F_{t}=\max_{k\geq t}U(A_{k},x) denote the highest payoff attainable from depth tt onward. A stopping classifier g⁡(Xt)∈{−1,+1}g(X_{t})\in\{-1,+1\} assigns +1+1 to stopping and −1-1 to continuing. It induces the stopping depth τ=min⁡({t<m:g⁡(Xt)=+1}∪{m}).\tau=\min\left(\{t<m:g(X_{t})=+1\}\cup\{m\}\right). For each nonterminal state, let Yt=+1Y_{t}=+1 when Δ⁡(St)≥0\Delta(S_{t})\geq 0 and Yt=−1Y_{t}=-1 otherwise. When Δ⁡(St)=0\Delta(S_{t})=0, stopping and continuing attain the same best payoff, and we assign the tie to stopping. The realized prefix regret is Regret⁡(g)=F0−U⁡(Aτ,x).\operatorname{Regret}(g)=F_{0}-U(A_{\tau},x).

Theorem 1 (Pathwise Prefix-Regret Decomposition)

For every task xx and stopping classifier gg,

Regret(g)=∑t=0min⁡{τ,m−1}|Δ(St)|𝟏{g(Xt)≠Yt}.\operatorname{Regret}(g)=\sum_{t=0}^{\min\{\tau,m-1\}}|\Delta(S_{t})|\mathbf{1}\{g(X_{t})\neq Y_{t}\}. (4)

Theorem 1 shows that realized regret is a sum of weighted mistakes, which motivates training against the regret-weighted classification risk defined below:

ℛ(g)=𝔼[|Δ(St)|⋅𝟏{g(Xt)≠Yt}].\mathcal{R}(g)=\mathbb{E}\bigl[\,|\Delta(S_{t})|\cdot\mathbf{1}\{g(X_{t})\neq Y_{t}\}\,\bigr]. (5)

4.2 Bayes Alignment of the Regret-Weighted Target

Theorem 2 (Bayes alignment for clairvoyant labels)

Any Bayes minimizer of ℛ⁡(g)\mathcal{R}(g) satisfies, almost surely on the event {𝔼[Δ(St)∣Xt]≠0}\{\mathbb{E}[\Delta(S_{t})\mid X_{t}]\neq 0\},

g∗​(Xt)=sign⁡(𝔼⁡[Δ⁡(St)∣Xt])g^{*}(X_{t})=\operatorname{sign}\bigl(\mathbb{E}[\Delta(S_{t})\mid X_{t}]\bigr)

Theorem 2 shows that weighting each error by the payoff at stake |Δ⁡(St)||\Delta(S_{t})| turns classification into payoff optimization. This is the Bayes rule of cost-sensitive learning (Elkan 2001), here instantiated for decision-focused stopping (Elmachtoub and Grigas 2022). It targets a different object than our predict-then-threshold baseline (Section 5), which estimates current sufficiency Pr⁡(Gx⊆At∣Xt)\Pr(G_{x}\subseteq A_{t}\mid X_{t}) and stops once predicted sufficiency clears a threshold. A perfectly calibrated sufficiency predictor can still stop at the wrong depth when cost is involved. In the training, we replace 0–1 loss with logistic loss while keeping the |Δ⁡(St)||\Delta(S_{t})| weights. The bounded weights act as a change of measure, so logistic calibration maintains the target decision boundary (Bartlett et al. 2006; Scott 2012; Elkan 2001). Lemma 2 in the appendix states the calibrated-surrogate result. We also note that Theorem 2 is an alignment result for the training target: it uses the clairvoyant gap Δ⁡(St)\Delta(S_{t}) and scores all prefix states, whereas the deployed policy sees only XtX_{t} and stops at the first predicted stop. We let the experiments measure the performance in the policy-level.

4.3 Marginal Value and the Limits of Sufficiency Prediction

Theorem 2 shows the optimal policy tracks sign⁡(𝔼⁡[Δ⁡(St)∣Xt])\operatorname{sign}\bigl(\mathbb{E}[\Delta(S_{t})\mid X_{t}]\bigr), while the following three results answer which observable features carry that sign. Proposition 1 reduces the stop/continue call to a marginal value-per-cost test, identifying the quantities a policy must estimate; Proposition 2 solves the decision in closed form under an additive-value benchmark; and Proposition 3 shows that this decision cannot be recovered from relevance scores alone once costs are heterogeneous. Together they imply what CAM-DF’s features must encode and why score-only rules are structurally insufficient.

Proposition 1 (One-step marginal rule)

For a nonterminal state StS_{t}, let jj be the tool at rank t+1t+1. Conditional on the observable features XtX_{t}, define

Vt=𝔼⁡[v⁡(At,Gx)∣Xt],Vt+1=𝔼⁡[v⁡(At∪{j},Gx)∣Xt].V_{t}=\mathbb{E}[v(A_{t},G_{x})\mid X_{t}],\quad V_{t+1}=\mathbb{E}[v(A_{t}\cup\{j\},G_{x})\mid X_{t}].

When comparing stopping at AtA_{t} with acquiring jj and then stopping, continuing is preferred if and only if Vt+1−Vtcj≥λ\frac{V_{t+1}-V_{t}}{c_{j}}\geq\lambda.

This proposition is a one-step comparison of the optimal prefix. Under the exact-sufficiency payoff UexactU_{\mathrm{exact}},

Vt+1−Vt=Pr⁡(Gx∖At={j}∣Xt),V_{t+1}-V_{t}=\Pr(G_{x}\setminus A_{t}=\{j\}\mid X_{t}),

the probability that the next tool completes the required set. Under this payoff, current-prefix sufficiency VtV_{t}, even if known exactly, does not by itself determine the preferred action: holding VtV_{t} fixed, differences in the completion probability or the next-tool cost can reverse the decision. Under the partial-coverage payoff UpartialU_{\mathrm{partial}}, Vt+1−VtV_{t+1}-V_{t} is the expected normalized coverage contributed by the next tool. In both cases the decision depends on the selected prefix, the next tool, and the remaining candidates.

Proposition 2 (Additive acquisition structure)

Suppose the expected non-cost value is additive, 𝔼⁡[v⁡(A,Gx)∣x]=∑j∈Apj​(x),\mathbb{E}[v(A,G_{x})\mid x]\allowbreak=\sum_{j\in A}p_{j}(x), where pj​(x)p_{j}(x) is the standalone value of tool jj. Under unconstrained subset acquisition, an optimal set keeps every tool whose value-per-cost clears the pressure,

A∗​(x)={j:pj​(x)cj≥λ}.A^{*}(x)=\left\{j:\frac{p_{j}(x)}{c_{j}}\geq\lambda\right\}.

Under the fixed score ordering, the optimal prefix depth is

t∗​(x)∈arg⁡max⁡∑r=1t0≤t≤m⁡(p(r)​(x)−λ​c(r)).t^{*}(x)\in\arg\max_{0\leq t\leq m}\sum_{r=1}^{t}\left(p_{(r)}(x)-\lambda c_{(r)}\right).

Consequently, at a nonterminal prefix AtA_{t}, continuing to some later prefix is strictly preferred if and only if

max⁡∑r=t+1kk>t⁡(p(r)​(x)−λ​c(r))>0.\max_{k>t}\sum_{r=t+1}^{k}\left(p_{(r)}(x)-\lambda c_{(r)}\right)>0.

With homogeneous costs and an ordering aligned with pj​(x)p_{j}(x), the fixed-prefix rule reduces to a value threshold, explaining why tuned score thresholds are strong in homogeneous-cost settings. Under heterogeneous costs, however, value-per-cost ratios need not follow the score ordering, and the optimal stopping depth depends on the cumulative surplus of later candidates. This structure motivates CAM-DF’s remaining tool score and cost features. Additivity is a tractable case with closed-form solution; the exact-sufficiency payoff instead couples tools through set completion, motivating learning rather than a fixed index policy.

Proposition 3 (Failure of score-monotone acquisition)

Under the additive model and the unconstrained-subset decision in Proposition 2, suppose two tools satisfy

pi​(x)>pj​(x)butpi​(x)ci<pj​(x)cj.p_{i}(x)>p_{j}(x)\qquad\text{but}\qquad\frac{p_{i}(x)}{c_{i}}<\frac{p_{j}(x)}{c_{j}}.

For any λ∈(pi​(x)ci,pj​(x)cj)\lambda\in\left(\frac{p_{i}(x)}{c_{i}},\frac{p_{j}(x)}{c_{j}}\right), the optimal cost-aware subset includes tool jj and excludes tool ii. Any rule monotone in value scores alone must include ii whenever it includes jj and therefore cannot reproduce this decision. Thus, under heterogeneous costs, score-only acquisition can be inconsistent with the cost-aware optimum.

Together, Propositions 2 and 3 show that acquisition decisions depend on marginal value relative to cost and, under a fixed ranking, on the cumulative net value of the remaining candidates. This structure motivates CAM-DF’s joint use of score, cost, and progress features.

4.4 Theory-Suggested Hypotheses

The structure above suggests when decision-focused stopping should pay. If scores perfectly separated the required from the non-required tools, a simple threshold would suffice; if they carried no signal, no stopping rule could help. In between, the gap between a payoff-aligned rule and a predict-then-threshold or score-only rule should widen with: (P1) score ambiguity, i.e. lower scorer AUC; (P2) cost dispersion, since varying costs make value-per-cost order diverge from score order (Propositions 2 and 3); (P3) cost pressure λ\lambda, since larger λ\lambda raises the regret of each unnecessary acquisition. Sections 6.1–6.3 test P1–P3 directly.

5 Method: CAM-DF and CAM-DF-lite

The theory motivates two components of CAM-DF. The sign and magnitude of the decision gap define the stop-or-continue label and its regret weight, while the marginal analysis motivates features that capture additional value relative to acquisition cost. CAM-DF combines these components in a supervised stopping classifier.

CAM-DF.

CAM-DF operationalizes Theorem 2 as an ℓ2\ell_{2}-regularized, regret-weighted logistic classifier. For each nonterminal prefix StS_{t}, t=0,…,m−1t=0,\ldots,m-1, the stop label is yt∗=𝟏{Δ(St)≥0}y_{t}^{*}=\mathbf{1}\{\Delta(S_{t})\geq 0\} and the sample weight is wt=|Δ⁡(St)|+ϵw_{t}=|\Delta(S_{t})|+\epsilon, where ϵ=10−4\epsilon=10^{-4} keeps zero-gap examples in training. Errors with larger payoff consequences therefore receive greater emphasis. Pooling the nonterminal prefixes from all training tasks yields NN training examples, each corresponding to one task at a particular candidate depth. CAM-DF models pθstop​(Xn)=σ⁡(θ0+θ⊤​ϕ​(Xn))p_{\theta}^{\mathrm{stop}}(X_{n})=\sigma(\theta_{0}+\theta^{\top}\phi(X_{n})) and minimizes

ℒ^​(θ)=1N​∑n=1N(|Δn|+ϵ)​ℓlog​(yn∗,pθstop​(Xn))+γ​‖θ‖22,\widehat{\mathcal{L}}(\theta)=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^{N}\bigl(|\Delta_{n}|+\epsilon\bigr)\ell_{\mathrm{log}}\left(y_{n}^{*},p_{\theta}^{\mathrm{stop}}(X_{n})\right)+\gamma\|\theta\|_{2}^{2}, (6)

where Δn\Delta_{n} and yn∗y_{n}^{*} denote the payoff gap and label of example nn, σ\sigma is the sigmoid function, ℓlog\ell_{\mathrm{log}} is binary logistic loss, and γ\gamma controls regularization. The feature map uses only scores, costs, prefix progress, and next-tool information available at deployment. The required-set annotation GxG_{x} enters training through the labels and weights, but not through the feature map. Further implementation details are summarized in Appendices B–C.

At deployment, CAM-DF scans candidate depths in increasing order and stops at the first state satisfying pθstop​(Xt)≥0.5p_{\theta}^{\mathrm{stop}}(X_{t})\geq 0.5. If no earlier state satisfies this condition, it selects the full ranked list. The scan occurs before execution and reveals no tool output. The downstream agent receives only the selected prefix.

CAM-DF-lite.

CAM-DF-lite is a lower-dimensional, interpretable variant of CAM-DF. Different from CAM-DF’s full feature map, it uses ten theory-motivated marginal score-cost and prefix-progress features. It predicts pθcont​(Xt)=Prθ⁡(Δ⁡(St)<0∣Xt)p_{\theta}^{\mathrm{cont}}(X_{t})=\Pr_{\theta}(\Delta(S_{t})<0\mid X_{t}) and stops when this probability falls below a validation-tuned threshold, whereas CAM-DF uses a fixed 0.50.5 stop gate. The decision target, loss, and prefix-scanning procedure are unchanged. Positive coefficients therefore favor further acquisition (Table A20).

6 Experiments

Datasets.

We use Retail as the primary benchmark and four additional domains to assess cross-domain generality (Table 1) (Yao et al. 2025; Bandi et al. 2026; Styles et al. 2024; Barres et al. 2025).

Baselines.

We compare against six baselines, each isolating a different acquisition signal. All tunable parameters are selected on validation payoff only.

  1. 1.

    Tuned fixed-kk: acquires the same validation-tuned number kk of top-ranked tools for every task.

  2. 2.

    Score threshold: acquires all tools with sj≥τs_{j}\geq\tau.

  3. 3.

    Score-per-cost threshold: independently acquires each tool satisfying sj/cj≥τs_{j}/c_{j}\geq\tau, providing a simple cost-aware heuristic motivated by Proposition 2.

  4. 4.

    Retail rule: selects tools using a hand-written mapping from request keywords and supplements this set with candidates passing a score threshold.

  5. 5.

    Predict-then-threshold: predicts whether the current prefix is sufficient and stops when exceeding a validation-tuned threshold (Jeong et al. 2024).

  6. 6.

    Aggregate-only DF: uses the CAM-DF objective with only aggregate summaries of the selected and remaining candidates, excluding next-tool and tool-identity features.

For reference, we also report a nondeployable prefix oracle that uses the true required set GxG_{x} to select the payoff-maximizing ranked prefix for each task, providing an upper bound for prefix-stopping policies.

Experimental setup.

The evaluation uses four shared settings:

  1. 1.

    Rankings: qwen-plus provides the primary rankings, which remain fixed during policy training and evaluation. Four additional frozen scorer configurations assess sensitivity to ranking quality.

  2. 2.

    Cost parameters: the main Retail analysis uses a 3×33\times 3 grid defined by cost pressure λ∈{0.05,0.12,0.20}\lambda\in\{0.05,0.12,0.20\} and cost dispersion d∈{0,1.0,1.5}d\in\{0,1.0,1.5\}, where dd controls the spread of costs around their mean and d=0d=0 is uniform.

  3. 3.

    Tuning: methods are selected by validation payoff over 30 random 55/20/25% train/validation/test splits (Atlas: 20 seeds; airline: 50; Appendix B).

  4. 4.

    Evaluation: we report payoff, sufficiency, acquisition cost, and paired task-bootstrap 95% confidence intervals using 2,000 resamples. All results except the live evaluation are offline replays.

Additional protocols and implementation details are provided in Appendices B and F.

6.1 Main Results

Performance across domains.

Table 2 reports the primary comparison at λ=0.12\lambda=0.12. On Retail, CAM-DF achieves the highest mean payoff at every tested cost dispersion and significantly outperforms Tuned fixed-kk and Predict-then-threshold throughout, setting a new state of the art among deployable tool-acquisition methods on this benchmark. The score-based thresholds remain competitive at this moderate cost pressure but do not match CAM-DF in mean payoff. CAM-DF-lite ranks second across all three Retail settings and first on MCP-Atlas, while CAM-DF ranks first on WorkBench and Telecom under heterogeneous costs. Airline remains inconclusive at n=28n=28, with the Score-per-cost threshold highest in mean. Figure 2 clarifies why task-specific stopping improves on a common acquisition depth. Under uniform costs, the post-hoc best common depth is k=5k=5, whereas task-optimal depths range from three to seven. CAM-DF achieves a mean payoff of 0.4000.400 with 4.344.34 tools on average, exceeding the common-depth maximum of 0.3000.300, while the prefix-oracle payoff of 0.5130.513 indicates remaining headroom.

Cost pressure and heterogeneity.

For comparative statics, we evaluate a denser 5×55\times 5 grid. CAM-DF outperforms Predict-then-threshold in mean in all 25 regimes, with paired-bootstrap 95% CIs above zero in 24. Gains increase consistently with λ\lambda and become largest at high dd, supporting P3 and providing directional support for P2; the peak is +0.21+0.21 at λ=0.20\lambda{=}0.20 and d=2d{=}2. Gains over Tuned fixed-kk narrow or reverse at the highest cost pressure, where a conservative common depth remains competitive (Figure 3; Table A18).

6.2 Ablation Study

Component and objective ablations.

The ablations separate the roles of state representation, the Δ\Delta-based objective, regret weighting, and model complexity. Restricting CAM-DF to aggregate prefix features lowers payoff by 0.0340.034–0.0510.051, with CIs excluding zero under heterogeneous costs (Table A14). Directly regressing Δ\Delta performs comparably to regret-weighted classification, with paired differences ranging from −0.006-0.006 to +0.025+0.025 and all CIs covering zero, while remaining above Predict-then-threshold in mean (Appendix D). This suggests that the main signal comes from targeting the stop-versus-continue payoff gap rather than from choosing classification over regression. Removing regret weights lowers payoff by 0.0340.034–0.0410.041 at λ=0.12\lambda{=}0.12, although the CIs cover zero, and by 0.0720.072–0.0790.079 at λ=0.05\lambda{=}0.05, where the CIs exclude zero. CAM-DF-lite remains within 0.0220.022–0.0270.027 of the full model, with all CIs covering zero. The no-identity variant also retains mean gains of +0.035/+0.045+0.035/+0.045 over Predict-then-threshold at d=1.0/1.5d{=}1.0/1.5. These results indicate that the gains are associated with Δ\Delta-targeted stopping and richer state information, without depending solely on model complexity or tool identity.

Value of learning across cost regimes.

We next examine when learned stopping improves on simple acquisition rules. At λ=0.12\lambda{=}0.12, CAM-DF significantly outperforms the direct plug-in sj≥λ​cjs_{j}\geq\lambda c_{j} by 0.0590.059–0.0710.071, while the fixed score rule sj≥0.5s_{j}\geq 0.5 remains statistically competitive. At λ=0.20\lambda{=}0.20 and d=1.5d{=}1.5, however, all four training-free rules lose significantly by 0.1000.100–0.2120.212 (Table A16). This boundary also appears on WorkBench and Telecom: the tuned Score-per-cost threshold is competitive under uniform costs, but CAM-DF leads under heterogeneous costs by 0.0080.008–0.0140.014 and 0.0670.067–0.0850.085, respectively (Tables A7 and A8). Additional controls show that CAM-DF’s advantage over Predict-then-threshold is robust to cost-vector permutations and symmetric tuning protocols (Appendix D).

6.3 Robustness and End-to-End Evaluation

Ranking-source robustness.

To test whether CAM-DF’s advantage depends on the qwen-plus ranking used in the main analysis, we rerun the full training and tuning pipeline under five frozen scorer configurations with required-tool AUCs ranging from 0.8350.835 to 0.9530.953. At λ=0.12\lambda{=}0.12, each scorer is evaluated under uniform and heterogeneous costs, yielding ten comparisons. CAM-DF exceeds the feature-matched, cost-inclusive Predict-then-threshold baseline in mean in all ten comparisons, with 95% CIs excluding zero in nine (Table A13). Gains are largest for the lowest-AUC scorer but do not vary monotonically across all five configurations, providing directional support for P1. Against the original score-only baseline, all ten gains have CIs excluding zero (Table A12).

End-to-end validation.

We test whether required-set sufficiency predicts realized task success and whether the learned policies reduce tool exposure in actual agent execution. On τ\tau-bench Retail, providing the annotated required set yields 0.670.67 success, whereas removing one required tool lowers success to 0.240.24 (p<0.001p{<}0.001), supporting the offline sufficiency proxy. CAM-DF and CAM-DF-lite achieve success rates of 0.670.67 and 0.640.64 while exposing only 4.44.4 and 4.34.3 of seven read tools, a 37%37\%–39%39\% reduction from full access, whose success rate is 0.580.58. Neither policy differs detectably from full access (McNemar p=0.21/0.42p{=}0.21/0.42), although these tests do not establish non-inferiority. An independent user simulator reproduces the pattern (Tables A5–A6).

7 Conclusion

This paper formulates pre-execution tool acquisition as a cost-aware stopping problem over ranked candidates. The CAM-DF family learns acquisition depth from stop-versus-continue payoff gaps through a regret-weighted objective with Bayes-alignment guarantees, and the marginal analysis characterizes when score-only acquisition is suboptimal. Experiments across five domains document payoff improvements across multiple ranking sources and cost regimes. The live Retail evaluation further demonstrates lower tool exposure with comparable observed task success. Together, these findings support cost-aware stopping as a modular control layer that converts an existing ranking into a decision without modifying the upstream ranker or underlying LLM. While CAM-DF provides a cost-aware framework for one-turn pre-execution acquisition, the current formulation does not update acquisition decisions after observing tool outputs. Extending the framework to output-adaptive multi-round settings always deserves attention.

Appendix A Proofs

A.1 Proof of Theorem 1

Write Ut=U⁡(St,x)U_{t}=U(S_{t},x) and Ft=maxk≥t⁡UkF_{t}=\max_{k\geq t}U_{k}. For every t<τt<\tau, the policy continues. If Yt=+1Y_{t}=+1, then Ft=UtF_{t}=U_{t} and

|Δ⁡(St)|=Ut−Ft+1=Ft−Ft+1.|\Delta(S_{t})|=U_{t}-F_{t+1}=F_{t}-F_{t+1}.

Because continuing disagrees with the stop label, this quantity is exactly the regret contribution at state tt. If Yt=−1Y_{t}=-1, then Ft=Ft+1F_{t}=F_{t+1}, and continuing incurs no regret contribution. Thus, for every t<τt<\tau,

|Δ(St)|𝟏{g(Xt)≠Yt}=Ft−Ft+1.|\Delta(S_{t})|\mathbf{1}\{g(X_{t})\neq Y_{t}\}=F_{t}-F_{t+1}.

Summing over the continuation states gives

∑t=0τ−1|Δ(St)|𝟏{g(Xt)≠Yt}=F0−Fτ.\sum_{t=0}^{\tau-1}|\Delta(S_{t})|\mathbf{1}\{g(X_{t})\neq Y_{t}\}=F_{0}-F_{\tau}.

If τ<m\tau<m, the policy stops at SτS_{\tau}. When Yτ=+1Y_{\tau}=+1, we have Fτ=UτF_{\tau}=U_{\tau}, so stopping incurs no regret. When Yτ=−1Y_{\tau}=-1, we have Fτ=Fτ+1>UτF_{\tau}=F_{\tau+1}>U_{\tau}, and

|Δ⁡(Sτ)|=Fτ+1−Uτ=Fτ−Uτ.|\Delta(S_{\tau})|=F_{\tau+1}-U_{\tau}=F_{\tau}-U_{\tau}.

Therefore,

|Δ(Sτ)|𝟏{g(Xτ)≠Yτ}=Fτ−Uτ.|\Delta(S_{\tau})|\mathbf{1}\{g(X_{\tau})\neq Y_{\tau}\}=F_{\tau}-U_{\tau}.

If τ=m\tau=m, there is no terminal decision term and Fm=UmF_{m}=U_{m}. Combining the continuation and stopping terms yields

F0−Uτ=∑t=0min⁡{τ,m−1}|Δ(St)|𝟏{g(Xt)≠Yt},F_{0}-U_{\tau}=\sum_{t=0}^{\min\{\tau,m-1\}}|\Delta(S_{t})|\mathbf{1}\{g(X_{t})\neq Y_{t}\},

which is the claimed identity. □\square

A.2 Proof of Theorem 2

Fix a feature value Xt=xX_{t}=x. If the classifier stops, the conditional risk is the expected weighted error incurred on states where continuing is better:

Rstop(x)=𝔼[|Δ(St)| 1{Δ(St)<0}∣Xt=x].R_{\mathrm{stop}}(x)=\mathbb{E}\bigl[\,|\Delta(S_{t})|\,\mathbf{1}\{\Delta(S_{t})<0\}\mid X_{t}=x\,\bigr].

If it continues,

Rcont(x)=𝔼[|Δ(St)| 1{Δ(St)≥0}∣Xt=x].R_{\mathrm{cont}}(x)=\mathbb{E}\bigl[\,|\Delta(S_{t})|\,\mathbf{1}\{\Delta(S_{t})\geq 0\}\mid X_{t}=x\,\bigr].

The Bayes rule stops iff Rstop​(x)≤Rcont​(x)R_{\mathrm{stop}}(x)\leq R_{\mathrm{cont}}(x), i.e.

𝔼[−Δ(St) 1{Δ(St)<0}∣Xt=x]≤𝔼[Δ(St) 1{Δ(St)≥0}∣Xt=x].\mathbb{E}\bigl[-\Delta(S_{t})\,\mathbf{1}\{\Delta(S_{t})<0\}\mid X_{t}=x\bigr]\\ \leq\mathbb{E}\bigl[\Delta(S_{t})\,\mathbf{1}\{\Delta(S_{t})\geq 0\}\mid X_{t}=x\bigr].

Rearranging, the two indicator terms combine into the full conditional expectation, so stopping is optimal iff 𝔼⁡[Δ⁡(St)∣Xt=x]≥0\mathbb{E}[\Delta(S_{t})\mid X_{t}=x]\geq 0. Hence any Bayes minimizer of ℛ⁡(g)\mathcal{R}(g) equals sign⁡(𝔼⁡[Δ⁡(St)∣Xt])\operatorname{sign}(\mathbb{E}[\Delta(S_{t})\mid X_{t}]). □\square

A.3 Deterministic Prefix Stopping Frontier

Lemma 1 (Finite-prefix stopping frontier)

Fix a task xx, a candidate order, and a payoff U⁡(Ak,x)U(A_{k},x) over prefixes A0,…,AmA_{0},\ldots,A_{m}. Let Ft=maxk≥t⁡U⁡(Ak,x)F_{t}=\max_{k\geq t}U(A_{k},x) be the best payoff attainable from state tt onward, with Fm=U⁡(Am,x)F_{m}=U(A_{m},x). At a nonterminal state t<mt<m, stopping is optimal among all later prefix depths iff

U⁡(At,x)≥Ft+1,U(A_{t},x)\geq F_{t+1},

equivalently iff Δ⁡(St)=U⁡(At,x)−maxk>t⁡U⁡(Ak,x)≥0\Delta(S_{t})=U(A_{t},x)-\max_{k>t}U(A_{k},x)\geq 0. The earliest optimal stopping depth is therefore min⁡{t:U⁡(At,x)=Ft}\min\{t:U(A_{t},x)=F_{t}\}.

Proof. The feasible continuation depths from state tt are exactly the finite set {t,t+1,…,m}\{t,t+1,\ldots,m\}. Stopping chooses depth tt and obtains U⁡(At,x)U(A_{t},x). Continuing at least once restricts the final depth to {t+1,…,m}\{t+1,\ldots,m\} and obtains at best Ft+1F_{t+1}. Thus stopping is optimal at tt iff its payoff is no smaller than the best payoff from all later prefixes. The stated equivalence follows from the definition of Δ⁡(St)\Delta(S_{t}), and the earliest optimal depth is the first index at which the running frontier FtF_{t} is attained by the current prefix. □\square

A.4 Weighted Logistic Surrogate

Lemma 2 (Logistic surrogate boundary)

Let Z=Δ⁡(St)Z=\Delta(S_{t}) and W=|Z|W=|Z|. Define Y∈{−1,+1}Y\in\{-1,+1\} by Y=+1Y=+1 iff Z≥0Z\geq 0, and assume 𝔼⁡[W∣X]<∞\mathbb{E}[W\mid X]<\infty. Fix X=xX=x and write a=𝔼[W𝟏{Y=+1}∣X=x]a=\mathbb{E}[W\mathbf{1}\{Y=+1\}\mid X=x], b=𝔼[W𝟏{Y=−1}∣X=x]b=\mathbb{E}[W\mathbf{1}\{Y=-1\}\mid X=x]; assume a,b>0a,b>0, so the conditional weighted logistic risk has a finite minimizer fxf_{x}. If 𝔼⁡[Z∣X=x]≠0\mathbb{E}[Z\mid X=x]\neq 0, then

sign⁡(fx)=sign⁡{𝔼⁡[Z∣X=x]}.\operatorname{sign}(f_{x})=\operatorname{sign}\{\mathbb{E}[Z\mid X=x]\}.

When instead a=0a=0 or b=0b=0 (conditionally pure labels), no finite minimizer exists; every sequence approaching the infimum has the stated sign eventually, and the ℓ2\ell_{2} regularization used in the implementation restores a finite minimizer with that sign.

Proof. For fixed xx, write a=𝔼[W𝟏{Y=+1}∣X=x]a=\mathbb{E}[W\mathbf{1}\{Y=+1\}\mid X=x] and b=𝔼[W𝟏{Y=−1}∣X=x]b=\mathbb{E}[W\mathbf{1}\{Y=-1\}\mid X=x]. With ℓy​(f)=log⁡{1+exp⁡(−y​f)}\ell_{y}(f)=\log\{1+\exp(-yf)\}, the conditional risk 𝔼⁡[W​ℓY​(f)∣X=x]\mathbb{E}[W\ell_{Y}(f)\mid X=x] is a​log⁡(1+e−f)+b​log⁡(1+ef)a\log(1+e^{-f})+b\log(1+e^{f}). When a,b>0a,b>0, its derivative is −a/(1+ef)+bef/(1+ef)-a/(1+e^{f})+be^{f}/(1+e^{f}), so the unique minimizer satisfies ef=a/be^{f}=a/b and has sign sign⁡(b)\operatorname{sign}(b). If a=0a=0 or b=0b=0, the infimum is approached at the corresponding infinite sign, which is why the lemma statement assumes a,b>0a,b>0. Since b=𝔼⁡[Z∣X=x]b=\mathbb{E}[Z\mid X=x], the weighted logistic population boundary matches the regret-weighted Bayes boundary. Finite-sample regularization affects estimation, not this population target. The ϵ=10−4\epsilon=10^{-4} weight floor of Algorithm C (numerical stability only) perturbs this population boundary by at most O⁡(ϵ)O(\epsilon): the implemented weights |Z|+ϵ|Z|+\epsilon shift bb to 𝔼⁡[Z∣X=x]+ϵ⁡(2​Pr⁡(Z≥0∣X=x)−1)\mathbb{E}[Z\mid X=x]+\epsilon\,(2\Pr(Z\geq 0\mid X=x)-1). □\square

A.5 Proof of Proposition 1

The two candidate actions yield expected payoffs Vt−λ​CtV_{t}-\lambda\,C_{t} (stop now) and Vt+1−λ⁡(Ct+cj)V_{t+1}-\lambda\,(C_{t}+c_{j}) (acquire jj, then stop), where CtC_{t} is the cost already sunk in AtA_{t}. Continuing is weakly better iff Vt+1−λ​Ct−λ​cj≥Vt−λ​CtV_{t+1}-\lambda C_{t}-\lambda c_{j}\geq V_{t}-\lambda C_{t}, i.e. Vt+1−Vt≥λ​cjV_{t+1}-V_{t}\geq\lambda c_{j}, equivalently (Vt+1−Vt)/cj≥λ(V_{t+1}-V_{t})/c_{j}\geq\lambda. □\square

For exact sufficiency, the non-cost value is v(A,G)=𝟏{G⊆A}v(A,G)=\mathbf{1}\{G\subseteq A\}. Adding next tool jj changes value by

v(A∪{j},G)−v(A,G)=𝟏{G⊆A∪{j}}−𝟏{G⊆A}.v(A\cup\{j\},G)-v(A,G)=\mathbf{1}\{G\subseteq A\cup\{j\}\}-\mathbf{1}\{G\subseteq A\}.

If AA is already sufficient this marginal is zero; if it is not, the marginal is one exactly when G∖A={j}G\setminus A=\{j\}. Thus the exact-payoff continuation value is about the probability that the next tool completes the remaining required set, not merely the probability that the next tool is individually relevant.

A.6 Proof of Proposition 2

Under the additive model the expected payoff of any AA is

𝔼⁡[U⁡(A,x)∣x]=∑j∈A(pj​(x)−λ​cj),\mathbb{E}[U(A,x)\mid x]=\sum_{j\in A}\bigl(p_{j}(x)-\lambda c_{j}\bigr),

a sum of per-tool terms that do not interact. The sum is maximized by including exactly the tools with nonnegative terms: j∈A∗​(x)j\in A^{*}(x) iff pj​(x)−λ​cj≥0p_{j}(x)-\lambda c_{j}\geq 0, i.e. pj​(x)/cj≥λp_{j}(x)/c_{j}\geq\lambda.

For the fixed-ordering parts: restricted to the score ordering, the only feasible sets are prefixes, and the prefix of depth tt has expected payoff ∑r=1t(p(r)​(x)−λ​c(r))\sum_{r=1}^{t}\bigl(p_{(r)}(x)-\lambda c_{(r)}\bigr) by the same additivity, so the optimal depth maximizes this partial sum. Continuing from depth tt to depth k>tk>t changes the expected payoff by ∑r=t+1k(p(r)​(x)−λ​c(r))\sum_{r=t+1}^{k}\bigl(p_{(r)}(x)-\lambda c_{(r)}\bigr); some continuation is strictly preferred to stopping at tt iff the maximum of these increments over k>tk>t is strictly positive, which is the stated condition. □\square

A.7 Proof of Proposition 3

By assumption pi>pjp_{i}>p_{j}, so any rule that ranks or thresholds on value scores alone admits ii whenever it admits jj. But pj/cj>pi/cip_{j}/c_{j}>p_{i}/c_{i}, so by Proposition 2 there exist cost pressures satisfying pi/ci<λ<pj/cjp_{i}/c_{i}<\lambda<p_{j}/c_{j} at which the optimal rule includes jj and excludes ii (the open interval avoids the boundary ties at either endpoint, where the optimum is not unique). On this range a rule that ranks or thresholds on value scores alone faces three cases, all of which disagree with the optimal cost-aware rule {j}\{j\}: a threshold τ≤pj\tau\leq p_{j} (or top-22 ranking) includes both, over-acquiring ii; a threshold satisfying pj<τ≤pip_{j}<\tau\leq p_{i} (or top-11 ranking) includes only ii, the exact inversion of the optimum; and a threshold τ>pi\tau>p_{i} excludes both, missing jj. □\square

A concrete two-tool instance makes the inversion visible. Let pi=0.8p_{i}=0.8, ci=4c_{i}=4, pj=0.5p_{j}=0.5, cj=1c_{j}=1, and λ=0.3\lambda=0.3. The score order prefers ii because 0.8>0.50.8>0.5. The cost-aware surplus terms are pi−λ​ci=−0.4p_{i}-\lambda c_{i}=-0.4 and pj−λ​cj=+0.2p_{j}-\lambda c_{j}=+0.2, equivalently pi/ci=0.2<λ<pj/cj=0.5p_{i}/c_{i}=0.2<\lambda<p_{j}/c_{j}=0.5. The optimal cost-aware subset is therefore {j}\{j\}, while any top-1 score rule chooses the wrong tool.

Appendix B Experimental Details

Retail cost vector.

Table A2 lists the base costs c¯\bar{c} before mean-normalization. This author-specified sensitivity vector is intended to encode that profile, order, and product lookups are operationally heavier than utility calls; it is not measured production telemetry. Dispersion-dd costs are cj​(d)=max⁡{0.10, 1+d⁡(c¯j/c¯mean−1)}c_{j}(d)=\max\{0.10,\;1+d(\bar{c}_{j}/\bar{c}_{\mathrm{mean}}-1)\}.

Splits and tuning.

Table A3 summarizes the split, tuning, hyperparameter, and bootstrap protocol. All thresholds and kk are tuned on validation payoff for each (λ,d,seed)(\lambda,d,\text{seed}); CAM-DF and all learned baselines are refit per split.

Pipeline reconciliation map.

Nominally identical comparisons can differ by small amounts across the released pipelines (for example, predict-then-threshold payoff 0.3520.352 in the main table versus 0.3610.361 in the Δ\Delta-regression rerun); every table caption names its pipeline, and all inference is within-pipeline paired. Table A4 maps each pipeline to the tables it feeds and to the features its predict-then-threshold baseline observes.

MCP-Atlas protocol.

Per seed, the sufficiency predictor (a ridge regressor under the partial payoff) and the CAM-DF-lite stopping classifier (regret-weighted logistic regression on the cost-free lite features) are refit on the training split. Candidates are each task’s listed tools (mean 15.2115.21, max 3737), with cj≡1c_{j}\equiv 1; paired bootstraps use the 485 tasks with complete policy pairs across all baselines.

Reproducibility.

All cached LLM scores (five Retail ranking configurations used to instantiate the interface; MCP-Atlas qwen-plus and qwen-turbo scores), cost vectors, seeds, and evaluation scripts are included in the anonymized release artifact. Every offline replay number in the paper is generated by the released pipeline; live execution numbers trace to released non-dry logs, with reruns requiring tau-bench setup and LLM/API credentials.

Using the training recipe outside replay.

Training needs required-set labels and a cost pressure. For prospective use, GxG_{x} could be mined from logged successful trajectories (the tools consulted before a verified correct action, our MCP-Atlas proxy) or labeled offline by judges, but trajectory-mined sets are noisy proxies that require audit or judge validation rather than automatic ground truth. The supervision-noise experiment shows the learned edge surviving roughly 5%5\% membership noise and inverting by 10%10\%, so verified rather than heuristic labels are the binding input. The cost pressure λ\lambda prices tool cost in units of task success. Operators can choose or sweep it against validation budget or latency constraints; Table A24 reports the full grid.

Appendix C Algorithmic and Prompt Details

This section spells out the implementation-facing details behind the CAM-DF training/inference recipe of main-text Section 5. It follows the same disclosure role as an appendix algorithm/prompt section: enough detail to reconstruct the replay target, the deployed gate, and the scoring interface without relying on prose interpretation.

C.1 Feature Inventory

The full CAM-DF feature map contains 39 public features in four groups. The aggregate selected/remaining block records prefix progress, selected and remaining score summaries, selected and remaining cost summaries, and selected/remaining score-per-cost totals. The marginal block records the next candidate’s score, cost, score/cost ratio, high-cost indicator, and related score-cost interactions. The cost-pressure block records dispersion and λ\lambda-scaled next-cost effects. The final optional identity block is a one-hot indicator for the next candidate tool; it is used only in full CAM-DF and is removed in CAM-DF-lite to reduce dependence on a fixed catalog.

CAM-DF-lite uses exactly ten features: progress t/mt/m; next score; next score divided by next cost; next-score gap to the second remaining candidate; remaining maximum score; normalized remaining-score sum; remaining score divided by remaining cost; normalized selected cost; λ\lambda times next cost; and the next-high-cost indicator. These are the features behind Table A20. They deliberately omit tool identity, offline labels, required-set size, and any outcome-derived information.

C.2 Retail Scoring Prompt Template

The prompt below is the default replay scorer template used to generate the qwen-style cached Retail necessity/value scores. It is an experimental way to populate the candidate-order interface; CAM-DF itself only requires a candidate order or score signal from some upstream harness component.

System/user prompt template. You are helping design a retail customer-service agent. The agent must decide which read-only information tools to call before taking any consequential business action such as cancel, return, exchange, or modify. Score each candidate tool from 0 to 1 for how necessary/useful it is for this specific user request. High score means the agent likely needs this tool before it can safely decide; low score means probably unnecessary. Do not score final mutation/action tools because they are not candidates here.

User request: [task id and user instruction]

Candidate read-only tools: [tool name and natural-language description for each candidate]

Return only a JSON object whose keys are exactly the tool names and whose values are numbers between 0 and 1. No explanation.

The conservative-prompt variant keeps the same input/output contract but asks for high scores only when a read-only tool is clearly needed before an irreversible business action. The score-generation temperature is 00 and cached JSONL rows store the task id, required set, and scores. Policy training and evaluation read those caches; no LLM call is needed to reproduce offline replay results.

C.3 Artifact and Implementation Trace

The implementation mirrors Algorithms C–C. Retail score caches live in the structured-tool-acquisition pilot results directory; selected older scorer caches are kept in that pilot’s legacy-results archive. CAM-DF, CAM-DF-lite, cross-scorer, ablation, tuning, label-noise, MCP-Atlas, MetaTool reduced-probe, and live-policy analysis scripts live in the tool-acquisition-correction scripts directory. The results digest is regenerated from frozen CSV/JSONL artifacts and is the single source of truth for manuscript numerals.

Appendix D Additional Robustness Checks

This appendix expands the five checks summarized in Section 6.2; all use the Retail benchmark.

Score order vs. sj/cjs_{j}/c_{j} order.

Proposition 3 indicts score-only orderings, yet CAM-DF acquires in score order, so we re-ran CAM-DF with acquisition re-ordered by sj/cjs_{j}/c_{j} (same labels, features, and loss). The orderings genuinely differ, selecting different prefixes on 65.6%65.6\% of λ=0.12\lambda=0.12 test tasks, but payoffs are statistically indistinguishable: paired differences (score minus sj/cjs_{j}/c_{j} order) at λ=0.12\lambda=0.12 are +0.000+0.000, +0.003+0.003, +0.007+0.007 for d=0,1.0,1.5d=0,1.0,1.5, all CIs covering zero (at d=0d=0 the orderings coincide). Table A15 reports the full λ×d\lambda\times d grid: no cell significantly favors the sj/cjs_{j}/c_{j} order (the most negative mean, −0.015-0.015 at λ=0.05\lambda=0.05, d=1.5d=1.5, has CI [−0.043,+0.003][-0.043,+0.003]), and at λ=0.20\lambda=0.20, d=1.5d=1.5 the score order is significantly better (+0.053+0.053, CI [+0.002,+0.098][+0.002,+0.098], task win rate 0.840.84). Re-ordering can even lower the attainable ceiling: the sj/cjs_{j}/c_{j}-order oracle payoff at d=1.5d=1.5 is 0.3850.385 versus 0.4190.419 under score order. In this Retail score-quality regime, cost awareness is carried mostly by the stopping layer, which absorbs much of the ordering difference; where dispersion and cost pressure are largest, the upstream ranking’s required-set signal is worth more than the sj/cjs_{j}/c_{j} re-weighting that scrambles it.

Δ\Delta-regression target.

To distinguish direct stopping-gap regression from regret-weighted classification, we regress Δ⁡(St)\Delta(S_{t}) on XtX_{t} and stop when the prediction is nonnegative. This performs on par with CAM-DF: paired differences are +0.025+0.025, +0.006+0.006, and −0.006-0.006 at λ=0.12\lambda=0.12, all with CIs covering zero. Like CAM-DF, it sits above predict-then-threshold stopping (0.372/0.319/0.2970.372/0.319/0.297 vs. 0.361/0.273/0.2350.361/0.273/0.235; both rerun within this experiment’s pipeline). We read this honestly: the gain comes from targeting the decision object Δ\Delta itself; the classification form adds the alignment of Theorem 2 and a slight edge under uniform cost.

Cost-vector perturbation.

The heterogeneous-cost results rest on an author-specified base cost vector, so we re-ran λ=0.12\lambda=0.12, d=1.0d=1.0 under 20 random permutations of the base costs across the seven tools (10 seeds each). CAM-DF beats predict-then-threshold stopping in 20 of 20 permutations (mean +0.059+0.059, range +0.027+0.027 to +0.110+0.110), with the per-permutation 95% CI excluding zero from above in 17 of 20 and never excluding zero from below; against the score-per-cost threshold the mean is +0.015+0.015, positive in only 65%65\% of permutations (negative mean in 7 of 20), with the CI excluding zero in just 2 of 20. The advantage over the learned baseline is robust to which tools happen to be expensive; against the tuned score-per-cost heuristic, what is robust is the main-setting statistical tie.

Tuning-protocol controls.

Baseline thresholds are tuned on a ≈{\approx}13-task validation split while CAM-DF uses a fixed 0.50.5 stop threshold, so part of the reported gaps could in principle be validation tuning noise. Symmetrizing the protocol either way says otherwise (Table A17). Giving CAM-DF a validation-tuned threshold does not help it: the tuned thresholds drift below the fixed 0.50.5 (per-dd medians 0.320.32/0.250.25/0.250.25) yet leave payoff unchanged. The differences for CAM-DF minus its tuned variant are +0.016+0.016/+0.018+0.018/+0.007+0.007 across dd, all with CIs covering zero, and payoff varies by less than 0.010.01 across fixed thresholds 0.30.3–0.50.5 at every dispersion. Denying the prediction baseline its tuning instead widens the gap to +0.070+0.070–+0.083+0.083 (CIs strictly positive). With both policies validation-tuned, the gap remains strictly positive (+0.030+0.030/+0.044+0.044/+0.060+0.060).

Training-free stopping predicates.

Training-free stopping rules (Kieback et al. 2026) argue for fixed predicates with no learned controller, so we evaluate four predicates whose parameters are fixed a priori and never see the train or validation split: (i) acquire every tool with sj≥0.5s_{j}\geq 0.5; (ii) cut the score-descending ranking at the largest adjacent score drop; (iii) take the smallest prefix holding 80%80\% of the total score mass; and (iv) the naive Proposition 2 plug-in acquiring jj iff sj≥λ​cjs_{j}\geq\lambda c_{j}, which treats the score as a calibrated marginal success probability. Predicates are evaluated on the same per-seed test splits as CAM-DF, so the paired task bootstrap is like-for-like (Table A16). CAM-DF beats the plug-in in 7 of 9 cells; the failure mechanism is systematic over-acquisition (sufficiency 0.970.97–0.980.98 at 5.35.3–6.46.4 tools versus CAM-DF’s 3.23.2–5.25.2), because raw scores are not calibrated marginal payoffs. At λ=0.20\lambda=0.20, d=1.5d=1.5 every predicate loses significantly (+0.100+0.100 to +0.212+0.212). The strongest predicate, the fixed 0.50.5 threshold, is a statistical tie at λ=0.12\lambda=0.12 (+0.022+0.022 to +0.034+0.034, CIs covering zero), consistent with the main-text boundary that simple rules are competitive at moderate pressure, while the predicates’ cost- and λ\lambda-blindness costs them exactly where cost pressure and heterogeneity bind.

Residual-corrected prediction (negative result).

If the gap were merely cost-related miscalibration of the sufficiency predictor, a double-machine-learning residual correction (Chernozhukov et al. 2018) should close it: we cross-fit a ridge model of the sufficiency residuals, corrected the prediction, and re-tuned the threshold. The diagnostic finds modest cost-related structure (mid-cost states over-predicted), but the corrected policy’s payoff is statistically indistinguishable from the uncorrected one (0.3660.366 vs. 0.3660.366 at d=0d=0; 0.2890.289 vs. 0.2850.285 at d=1.0d=1.0; 0.2470.247 vs. 0.2470.247 at d=1.5d=1.5) and stays below the same-pipeline decision-focused policy (CAM-DF rerun within this experiment: 0.3700.370, 0.2900.290, 0.2690.269; SEs ≤0.015\leq 0.015) at every dispersion. Fixing the prediction is not fixing the decision.

LLM self-selection reference.

As a descriptive reference (one prompt, all 67 tasks, no splits, not a tuned competitor), we let qwen-plus itself choose the tool set given the task, tools, costs, and λ=0.12\lambda=0.12. It under-acquires substantially (sufficiency 0.390.39/0.310.31 at d=0d=0/1.01.0, payoffs +0.024+0.024/−0.121-0.121, versus 0.4000.400/0.3310.331 for CAM-DF on the same scores), consistent with cost-centric agent evaluations (Liu et al. 2025b; Liu et al. 2025a): the LLM does not self-manage acquisition under cost pressure.

Appendix E End-to-End Execution on Retail

The main payoff scores an acquired set by the sufficiency indicator 𝟏{Gx⊆A}\mathbf{1}\{G_{x}\subseteq A\} rather than by running the agent. To check that this proxy tracks realized task success, we execute acquired sets in the live τ\tau-bench Retail benchmark: qwen-plus serves as both the tool-calling agent and the user simulator (temperature 00, up to 3030 steps), and tau-bench scores each episode 0/10/1 by checking the resulting database state. The agent’s read-only tools are restricted to a set AA while all write/action tools remain available, so the experiment isolates the effect of read-tool acquisition on real success. We compare five per-task conditions over all 6767 tasks (Table A5): full (AA = all seven read candidates), oracle (A=GxA=G_{x}), insufficient (A=GxA=G_{x} minus its lowest-scored required tool), and the CAM-DF/CAM-DF-lite acquired sets from the main λ=0.12,d=1.0\lambda=0.12,d=1.0 policy configuration.

Realized success tracks the proxy. Giving the agent only the required read tools (oracle) shows no detectable benefit from the extra four tools relative to all seven (full): 0.670.67 vs 0.580.58, a paired McNemar test on the shared 67 tasks not rejecting equality (p=0.21p=0.21; if anything favoring oracle, oracle-only-win 1111 vs full-only-win 55, plausibly because fewer distractor tools focus the agent; this is an underpowered null at n=67n=67, not a proven equivalence). Dropping a single required tool collapses success from 0.670.67 to 0.240.24 (oracle wins 3434 tasks, insufficient 55; p<0.001p<0.001), even though the insufficient agent issues fewer tool calls (5.05.0 vs 6.66.6): under-acquisition is cheaper but fails. The proxy is not conservative: the dropped (lowest-scored) required tool is load-bearing for real success. It is also not perfect (insufficient still succeeds on 24%24\% of tasks, where the agent works around the missing tool or the used-tools annotation slightly overstates the minimal set), but the gap between proxy-sufficient and proxy-insufficient acquisitions (0.630.63 vs 0.240.24) supports 𝟏{Gx⊆A}\mathbf{1}\{G_{x}\subseteq A\} as a useful end-to-end success proxy and suggests that GxG_{x} coverage is often sufficient in this harness. The learned policy rows close the dry-run boundary: CAM-DF succeeds on 0.670.67 (45/67) and CAM-DF-lite on 0.640.64 (43/67), both far above insufficient acquisition (CAM-DF policy-only wins 2929 tasks vs 00 insufficient-only; CAM-DF-lite 3030 vs 33; exact p<0.001p<0.001). Task-level diagnostics support the same bounded reading rather than a tautological proxy story: CAM-DF acquires exactly GxG_{x} on 29 tasks, a strict superset on 34, and misses at least one annotated required read tool on 4; its proxy/live cells are 41 covered successes, 22 covered failures, 4 missing-but-successful tasks, and 0 missing failures. CAM-DF-lite gives the analogous 28/31/8 exact/superset/missing split, with 41 covered successes, 18 covered failures, 2 missing-but-successful tasks, and 6 missing failures. Mean tool calls do not explain success monotonically (CAM-DF success/failure calls 6.89/7.326.89/7.32; CAM-DF-lite 6.65/6.506.65/6.50), so the live check is about information sufficiency rather than simply calling more tools. The acquisition-side saving is visible in exposure: the policies provision 4.394.39/4.314.31 of the seven read tools on average (full access provisions all 77) at statistically indistinguishable success: exposure is the cost object the stopping layer controls, while realized call counts are the downstream agent’s choice and stay comparable. The policy rows do not prove live dominance over full/oracle access: CAM-DF vs full has exact p=0.210p=0.210, CAM-DF vs oracle p=1.000p=1.000, CAM-DF-lite vs full p=0.424p=0.424, and CAM-DF-lite vs oracle p=0.804p=0.804.

Independent user-simulator replication.

Because qwen-plus serves as both agent and user simulator above (self-play, temperature 00), we reran all five conditions with qwen-max as the user simulator, holding the agent model and every acquired set fixed (Table A6). The pattern replicates: insufficient acquisition collapses to 0.210.21 (14/67), the learned policies reach 0.630.63 (CAM-DF, 42/67) and 0.640.64 (CAM-DF-lite, 43/67), and full/oracle sit at 0.660.66 (44/67). Paired exact tests under the independent simulator: CAM-DF beats insufficient 29-policy-only-wins to 1 (p<0.001p<0.001; CAM-DF-lite 29 to 0), while policies remain statistically indistinguishable from full/oracle (CAM-DF vs full p=0.727p=0.727, vs oracle p=0.727p=0.727; CAM-DF-lite p=1.000p=1.000 for both). One simulator-dependent detail is worth noting honestly: under qwen-max the full-tool condition improves from 0.580.58 to 0.660.66, so the self-play run’s suggestion that distractor tools hurt the full agent does not replicate; none of our claims rests on that comparison. The remaining live caveats are the single scorer/cost setting and the ranked-prefix (not online multi-round) scope.

The caveats are therefore narrower but still important: the policy check covers one scorer/cost setting, and the experiment is still ranked-prefix acquisition rather than online multi-round control.

Appendix F Cross-Domain Scale and Replication Details

This appendix expands the cross-domain scale test of Section 6.1. All three domains use the identical replay pipeline as Retail: candidates ordered by frozen qwen-plus necessity scores, exact and partial payoff, cost dispersions d∈{0,1.0,1.5}d\in\{0,1.0,1.5\}, λ∈{0.05,0.12,0.20}\lambda\in\{0.05,0.12,0.20\}, 30 splits (50 for airline), and a task-level paired bootstrap. The complete per-cell grids are in the released results digest; the tables below report the main cost pressure λ=0.12\lambda=0.12.

WorkBench (statistical-power domain).

WorkBench (Styles et al. 2024) is an outcome-centric agent benchmark whose grading compares the final sandbox database state to a per-task ground-truth outcome. We use its 13 read-only information tools as the candidate pool (the 14 write tools are the consequential action, not candidates, matching the Retail/τ2\tau^{2} convention) and obtain 639 usable tasks after removing tasks with no read requirement. Because the gold outcome records only write calls, the required-read set is not lifted from a gold read trajectory; it is the per-task majority consensus of the read calls issued by five strong reference agents whose write calls match the gold outcome (cross-model pairwise Jaccard 0.930.93–0.990.99). This is a derived label, weaker than a human-read gold trajectory but stable across models; it is disclosed here and in the artifact, not silently treated as ground truth. The scorer is strong on this domain (AUC 0.9820.982, cover-all rank 2.012.01 of 1313, mean required-set size 1.641.64). Table A7 shows the λ=0.12\lambda=0.12 result: against the tuned score-per-cost and score thresholds the paired gap covers zero under exact payoff at uniform cost (matching Retail) but excludes zero under heterogeneous cost and under partial payoff at every dispersion, with the effect small (+0.006+0.006 to +0.014+0.014). The pattern holds across λ\lambda: at λ=0.05\lambda=0.05 the exact heterogeneous-cost score-per-cost cells are negative (the cost-blind ranking is well tuned at low pressure), and at λ=0.20\lambda=0.20 they are positive again, while the predict-then-threshold gap is positive at all three pressures under heterogeneous cost.

τ2\tau^{2}-bench airline (low-power replication).

τ2\tau^{2}-bench (Barres et al. 2025) is a dual-control tool-agent benchmark; we extract its airline domain (28 usable tasks, 6 read-only candidate tools, required mean 1.681.68, qwen-plus scorer AUC 0.9030.903 / qwen-max 0.9160.916). With only 28 tasks the CIs are wide, so this is a replication check, not a powered comparison. CAM-DF significantly beats the non-learning heuristics that ignore cost structure: against acquiring all candidates the gap is +0.228+0.228 to +0.255+0.255 at λ=0.12\lambda=0.12 (all CIs positive), and against tuned fixed-kk it is significant at λ=0.20\lambda=0.20 under uniform and high-dispersion cost. Against the strongest learned baselines (predict-then-threshold stopping, Aggregate-only DF) and the tuned score-per-cost threshold the CIs cover zero, as expected at this sample size (Table A8).

τ2\tau^{2}-bench telecom (dual-model proxy labels).

The telecom domain (114 usable tasks, 21 read-only candidate tools, required mean 5.545.54) is our largest-required-set domain. To avoid a single model both labeling and scoring, required sets are shadow-labeled by qwen-max and necessity scores are produced by qwen-plus; the reported AUC 0.9430.943 therefore measures two-model agreement, not recovery of a human gold set, and we read telecom as MCP-Atlas-level proxy evidence rather than a gold benchmark. Telecom is an exact-payoff-hard domain: with required mean 5.545.54 and λ=0.20\lambda=0.20, even the oracle often prefers acquiring nothing, so the exact-payoff comparisons degenerate. The informative cells are heterogeneous-cost and partial payoff, where CAM-DF beats Aggregate-only DF, its cost-blind twin (partial +0.020+0.020 [+0.015,+0.025][+0.015,+0.025] at d=1.0d=1.0; +0.022+0.022 [+0.017,+0.027][+0.017,+0.027] at d=1.5d=1.5) and the tuned score-per-cost threshold under partial payoff at d=1.0d=1.0 (+0.036+0.036 [+0.027,+0.046][+0.027,+0.046]); at uniform cost the tuned score-per-cost rule leads (−0.021-0.021 exact, −0.013-0.013 partial), the honest boundary for a hard set-coverage domain (Table A8).

G.1 Scores and Payoff Definitions

G.2 Robustness, Ablations, and Tuning

The coefficient table ties the robustness checks back to the mechanism claim. CAM-DF-lite does not need hidden labels or tool identities at deployment time: its dominant directions are the score-side continuation terms and the cost-side stopping terms predicted by the marginal rule.

G.3 External Validation and Complete Numeric Readouts

Heterogeneous costs on MCP-Atlas: independent replication.

Independently of the ten-vector replay above (Table A22), we rerun the Atlas replay under a second cost-randomization design: per seed, one base cost per distinct tool name is drawn from Uniform⁡(0.5,2.0)\mathrm{Uniform}(0.5,2.0) (the range spanned by the Retail base costs) and interpolated with the Retail dispersion rule cj​(d)=max⁡{0.10, 1+d⁡(c¯j/c¯mean−1)}c_{j}(d)=\max\{0.10,\,1+d(\bar{c}_{j}/\bar{c}_{\mathrm{mean}}-1)\}, with λ∈{0.05,0.12,0.20}\lambda\in\{0.05,0.12,0.20\} and 20 seeds. The cost-augmented features are constant at d=0d=0, so the d=0d=0 models coincide with the homogeneous-cost pipeline (a built-in sanity check). Table A23 reports the cost-augmented stopping policy against its cost-blind lite twin and the tuned score-per-cost threshold. Against the cost-blind twin, all six heterogeneous partial-payoff cells are positive with CIs excluding zero, growing with dispersion; under exact payoff the tuned score-per-cost threshold flips from ahead at d=0d=0 to behind at d=1.5d=1.5 (+0.034+0.034 [+0.022,+0.046][+0.022,+0.046] at λ=0.12\lambda=0.12; +0.073+0.073 [+0.068,+0.079][+0.068,+0.079] at λ=0.20\lambda=0.20). The honest boundary is the partial-payoff, high-dispersion corner, where the non-prefix score-per-cost rule wins (−0.042-0.042 [−0.049,−0.035][-0.049,-0.035] at λ=0.20\lambda=0.20, d=1.5d=1.5): partial credit rewards skipping expensive mid-ranking tools, which a prefix policy cannot do. Prefix stopping is robust under exact sufficiency; under partial credit with extreme heterogeneity, non-prefix marginal rules become the stronger competitor, again evidence that the marginal value/cost structure, rather than the specific policy class, carries the gain.

MetaTool reduced boundary check.

MetaTool (Huang et al. 2024) is a useful stress test for whether a query-to-tool label benchmark can support our acquisition abstraction, but it is not a native cost-aware stopping benchmark: the public multi-tool subset gives two required tools per query, not live tool outputs, operational costs, or a downstream task reward. We therefore ran a no-API reduced replay on the 497-task corpus with the 15 tools appearing as required in that subset, unit costs, exact sufficiency, and an unsupervised train-split TF-IDF cosine scorer (full-fit diagnostic AUC 0.7650.765, mean cover-all rank 6.826.82). The 30 random 60/20/20 splits place 100 tasks in each test fold and cover 496 unique tasks in the paired bootstrap table. The result is deliberately not used as main evidence. At λ=0.12\lambda=0.12, CAM-DF-lite beats predict-then-threshold stopping by +0.026+0.026 [+0.002,+0.050][+0.002,+0.050], but is not better than fixed-kk (−0.009-0.009 [−0.025,+0.005][-0.025,+0.005]) or score threshold (−0.014-0.014 [−0.031,+0.002][-0.031,+0.002]). This check supports the boundary stated in the main paper: CAM-DF needs a meaningful ranking signal and payoff/cost labels; shallow homogeneous-cost tool-selection labels are not enough to claim a third positive benchmark.
